Disability benefit offsets: map the retroactive award, repayment and ongoing income

Four interactive charts reconcile an invented monthly offset, past overlapping benefit periods, a retroactive award and the cash earmarked for repayment before tax.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Reconcile two invented benefit sources and a retroactive payment

Interactive planning lab

Combined ongoing monthly amount after the assumed offset · before tax$4,000
Modeled repayment for past overlapping months · before tax$7,200
Retroactive award less modeled repayment · before tax$0

Original hypothetical CAD illustration of gross payments, not an actual disability award, insurance quotation, CPP calculation or universal coordination rule. Source B is assumed eligible for the entered offset. Plan A is reduced by the selected percentage of B, capped at A’s original monthly amount so A cannot become negative. Both past payment histories end immediately before B’s receipt; only the shorter trailing window overlaps. A was assumed paid in full for its entered past months, and the revised offset applies retrospectively only to overlapping months. B’s gross retroactive award covers its entered prior months. Day 0 is after award receipt; full repayment occurs at the end of the selected lag day. If lag is zero, the first point is after both same-day transactions and no intraday peak is shown. The calendar isolates the retroactive award, the unpaid repayment earmark and their residual. It excludes starting household cash, spending, regular ongoing benefits, tax, withholding, fees, interest, instalment repayments and borrowing. The residual is not verified spendable net cash. No eligibility assessment, overall-income ceiling, source exclusion, indexation, repayment deadline or tax relief is estimated. Actual documents determine the coordination basis, covered dates and repayment amount.

The central idea

Check coordination before adding income sources. Match a retroactive receipt with any confirmed repayment, then assess tax and other commitments before treating the residual as household cash.

01

Identify which payment changes when another source begins

Two benefit letters do not necessarily describe two amounts that can simply be added. A plan may reduce its payment when another income source begins, and a later approval may cover months for which the first plan already paid.

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada explains that many long-term disability plans reduce benefits when other disability income is received. Service Canada also notes that other payers may adjust their payments following CPP disability approval. Neither statement supplies a universal formula for every contract.

The charts therefore use an invented Plan A and Source B. Every amount is gross CAD before tax and withholding. No CPP award, insurer quotation or medical eligibility decision is estimated. The purpose is to separate monthly coordination, past entitlement and cash movement before updating a budget.

02

Calculate the reduction before adding the ongoing amounts

The default assumes Plan A pays CAD 4,000 per month before coordination and Source B pays CAD 1,200. The entered offset is 100% of B, so A falls by CAD 1,200 to CAD 2,800. The ongoing combined amount is CAD 4,000 before tax, rather than CAD 5,200.

The authored reduction is the smaller of A’s original amount and B multiplied by the entered percentage. That cap prevents A from becoming negative. It is a calculation convention for this page, not a claim that every plan uses this rule or lacks other limits.

At a 50% assumption, A falls by CAD 600 and the combined monthly amount becomes CAD 4,600. At 0%, no A reduction is modeled. These are alternatives for understanding the arithmetic; changing the control does not establish which treatment a real contract permits, and no overall-income ceiling is modeled.

03

Match the months covered by each source before calculating a repayment

In the default, A was paid in full for six prior months, totaling CAD 24,000. B’s retroactive award covers the same six months and equals CAD 7,200. Applying the assumed monthly reduction to those overlapping months produces a CAD 7,200 A overpayment and revised A entitlement of CAD 16,800.

The stacked bars partition the original A cash. The overpayment is already inside that CAD 24,000; it is not another receipt. B’s later award is a separate cash event with a separate possible repayment obligation.

Both histories are assumed to end immediately before B’s receipt. Their shorter duration determines overlap. If A paid only three prior months while B’s award covers six, the modeled repayment is CAD 3,600 and B’s gross residual is CAD 3,600. Months before A began paying create no A overpayment under this invented rule. Real start dates and exclusions still need their own review.

04

Track the receipt and the unpaid obligation on the same calendar

The calendar isolates the retroactive award. Under the default, day zero ends with CAD 7,200 received and CAD 7,200 earmarked for repayment. The cash balance is larger, but cash less that obligation is zero before considering any tax.

The full modeled repayment occurs at the end of day thirty. Cash then falls to zero and the unpaid earmark also becomes zero. The residual does not fall a second time. Keeping a repayment reserve after the liability has already been paid would count the same obligation twice.

A zero-day lag shows the balance after both same-day transactions; it does not display a temporary intraday peak. The chosen lag is hypothetical and does not set a lawful or contractual repayment deadline. Ordinary monthly benefits, household spending, starting savings, interest and withholding are excluded from this isolated ledger, so it is not a complete bank-account forecast.

05

Use the actual plan’s coordination terms and confirmed reconciliation

A concrete official example appears in the federal public-service Disability Insurance guidelines. They explain that a retroactive award from another source may create an overpayment that must be reimbursed. Those instructions concern that particular plan, not every employer or individual policy.

The same guidance states that income from a private individual disability plan does not reduce its DI payment. That specific exception shows why the source of the money matters. It should not be generalized to other contracts, nor should this page’s offset control be treated as a determination of the federal plan’s rules.

For an actual reconciliation, identify the income source, the dates it covers, what the first payer already paid and the confirmed adjustment. An award receipt date alone cannot establish the period of overlap. The charts assume both histories end together; separated or interrupted benefit periods require a dated calculation beyond this model.

06

Carry the revised receipts and confirmed obligation into a separate budget

Keep ongoing monthly payments separate from a one-time retroactive award. Updating the monthly budget to the sum of two unadjusted letters could overstate future receipts. Treating the entire lump sum as a windfall could also overlook a repayment relating to earlier months.

The matrix varies the assumed offset and B’s covered period while holding A’s payment history fixed. A larger residual may simply reflect B covering months before A began paying. It does not establish a more suitable policy or an entitlement that has been approved.

Finally, distinguish gross figures from confirmed net cash. This tool calculates no tax liability, withholding, tax deduction or refund. If deductions apply to an award, its gross entitlement and the deposit can differ. Compare the actual transfer with the confirmed repayment request before assuming the new deposit alone funds everything due. Use the actual payer statements and confirmed repayment before allocating money, then account separately for tax and other obligations. The related waiting-period and illness-payment guides address broader household cash calendars; this page isolates the coordination arithmetic that must be resolved before those receipts are entered.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All four charts use original hypothetical CAD amounts and coordination assumptions. Official sources explain that offsets and retrospective overpayments can occur; the model does not reproduce a specific plan or calculate benefit eligibility or tax. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. FCAC · Disability insurance ↗

    Page dated 31 July 2026; reviewed 25 October 2026. Supports checking benefit coordination, definitions and tax treatment. It does not establish a universal offset formula. All chart amounts and percentages are independently authored assumptions.

  2. Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat · Disability insurance guidelines ↗

    Page dated 8 May 2026; reviewed 25 October 2026. Reporting additional sources of income section describes retroactive awards, possible overpayments and reimbursement for this federal public-service plan, including its specific individual-policy exception. This example is not applied to other plans or personal accounts.

  3. Service Canada · CPP disability benefits: how much you could receive ↗

    Page dated 13 October 2026; reviewed 25 October 2026. The other-income section notes that other payers may change their payments following CPP disability approval. No government benefit amount, maximum, contribution history or eligibility test is copied into the illustration.
